label: Yirmeyahu (Jeremiah) — Part 6 — Chapters 40–48
summary_plain: After the fall of Yerushalayim, Nebukhadnetzar leaves Gedalyahu son of Achikam as governor over the remnant in the land. Yirmeyahu is released from chains and stays with Gedalyahu at Mitzpah. Yishma'EL son of Netanyahu assassinates Gedalyahu and kills the garrison. Yochanan son of Qareach pursues Yishma'EL and rescues the captives. The remnant asks Yirmeyahu to inquire of YHWH — he says: Stay in this land and do not go down to Mitsrayim. But they refuse to obey YHWH's voice and flee to Mitsrayim, taking Yirmeyahu with them. In Mitsrayim, the women burn incense to the Queen of Heaven and say: When we burned incense to her, we had plenty of food and were well. Yirmeyahu delivers oracles against Mitsrayim, Moav, Ammon, Edom, Damascus, Qedar, Chatsor, and Elam.
summary_scholarly: The ACR reads from the DSS Jeremiah manuscripts (4QJer-a through 4QJer-e) and the Orit Ge'ez. Chapters 40-44 document the aftermath of the Babylonian destruction — the remnant community's decision to flee to Mitsrayim against YHWH's explicit command. The Queen of Heaven worship in chapter 44 records the women's defense of syncretic practice — they claim prosperity came through her veneration, not through YHWH's covenant. The LXX arrangement of Jeremiah differs significantly from the Masoretic in these chapters — the oracles against the nations (chapters 46-48 in the MT) appear in a different position in the LXX, and the DSS fragments support the shorter LXX text type. The flight to Mitsrayim inverts the exodus pattern: the covenant people voluntarily return to the house of bondage.

key_terms.definition: After Yerushalayim's fall, Nebuchadnezzar appointed Gedalyahu ben Akhikam governor over the remaining population; Yirmeyahu chose to stay in the land with him at Mitzpah.

Yishma'el ben Netanyah, of royal blood, killed Gedalyahu and all the Yehudim with him at Mitzpah, also killing Babylonian soldiers; this act destroyed the remnant community's last stability in the land.

After Gedalyahu's assassination, the surviving remnant asked Yirmeyahu whether to flee to Mitzrayim; YHWH through Yirmeyahu commanded them to stay in the land; they fled to Mitzrayim anyway, taking Yirmeyahu with them.
YHWH declares: if you go to Mitzrayim, the sword, famine, and pestilence that you fear in Yehudah will overtake you in Mitzrayim; the land you fear will find you in the land you fled to.
Yirmeyahu 46 addresses the defeat of Pharaoh Nekho at Carchemish (605 BCE) by Nebuchadnezzar; YHWH says Mitzrayim shall be put to shame by Babylon — the great river kingdom will be humbled.
In Mitzrayim, the Yehudite women (and their husbands) burn incense to the Queen of Heaven; when Yirmeyahu rebukes them, they say things went better when they worshipped her and refuse to stop.

Yirmeyahu's devoted scribe; Yirmeyahu 45 addresses Barukh directly with a personal promise: 'I will give you your life as a prize of war in all places to which you may go.' He preserved Yirmeyahu's scroll.

YHWH commanded Yirmeyahu to dictate all his prophecies; Barukh wrote them on a scroll, which was read in the Temple, then to the princes, then to King Yehoyaqim, who cut it and burned it; Yirmeyahu and Barukh rewrote it with more additions.
Chapters 46-51 of Yirmeyahu contain oracles against Mitzrayim, Plishtim, Moav, Ammon, Edom, Damascus, Qedar, Khatzor, Elam, and Babylon; YHWH's judgment extends over every regional power.

Yirmeyahu 48 is the longest oracle against a single nation in the book; Moav is condemned for pride and self-confidence in its own strength ('I am mighty and strong'); YHWH will humble Kemosh the god of Moav.

faq.question: Who was Gedalyahu and why was his appointment significant?
faq.answer: Gedalyahu ben Akhikam was appointed by Nebuchadnezzar as governor over the peasants and poor left in Yehudah after the exile. His father Akhikam had earlier protected Yirmeyahu's life (Yirmeyahu 26:24). Yirmeyahu chose to stay with Gedalyahu — a sign that living faithfully under Babylonian authority was possible. Gedalyahu's assassination by Yishma'el destroyed the last organized remnant in the land.

faq.question: Why did the remnant go to Mitzrayim against YHWH's word?
faq.answer: After Gedalyahu's murder, the people feared Babylonian retaliation. They asked Yirmeyahu to inquire of YHWH and promised to obey whatever he said. YHWH's answer was clear: stay in the land, do not fear Babylon, I will protect you there. But they accused Yirmeyahu of lying and fled to Mitzrayim anyway, taking Yirmeyahu and Barukh with them. Their fear of Babylon was stronger than their trust in YHWH.

faq.question: What is the theological significance of the Queen of Heaven passage in Yirmeyahu 44?
faq.answer: The women in Mitzrayim argue explicitly that things went better when they burned incense to the Queen of Heaven — prosperity and safety. When they stopped, disaster came. This is a direct theological counter-argument to Yirmeyahu's covenant theology. YHWH answers: you stopped burning incense to other gods only partially and inconsistently — it was your unfaithfulness to the whole covenant that brought disaster, not stopping the Queen of Heaven worship.

faq.question: Why is Barukh's oracle in Yirmeyahu 45 addressed to him personally?
faq.answer: Yirmeyahu 45 is a brief oracle specifically for Barukh: 'Do not seek great things for yourself in a time when I am bringing disaster on all flesh.' Barukh is apparently discouraged and perhaps mourning the loss of his expectations. YHWH's promise to him — 'I will give you your life as a prize of war' — is humble but real: survival is itself the gift in this season, not prosperity or advancement.

faq.question: What is the significance of King Yehoyaqim burning Yirmeyahu's scroll?
faq.answer: Yehoyaqim's burning of the scroll (chapter 36) is a paradigm of the rejection of YHWH's word by power. The king heard three or four columns and cut them off with a knife and threw them in the fire — a deliberate, unhurried rejection, not a moment of rage. YHWH's response: Yehoyaqim will have no descendant on David's throne; he himself will be thrown out unburied. And the scroll was rewritten with more words added.

faq.question: What did the oracle against Mitzrayim in Yirmeyahu 46 teach about Pharaoh's power?
faq.answer: Yirmeyahu 46 describes the defeat of Pharaoh Nekho's army at Carchemish (605 BCE) in real historical terms: the soldiers flee, the mighty are stumbled, the shield-bearer is paralyzed. YHWH uses this historical disaster to demonstrate that Mitzrayim's military power — the thing the Yehudites fled to for protection — cannot save them. If Mitzrayim cannot defend itself at Carchemish, it cannot protect the Yehudite refugees.

faq.question: What is the oracle against Moav in Yirmeyahu 48 about?
faq.answer: Yirmeyahu 48 is the longest single-nation oracle in the book. Moav is condemned primarily for pride: 'I am mighty and strong' (48:14); 'you trusted in your works and your treasures' (48:7). YHWH will humble Kemosh (Moav's national deity) and send Moav into exile. Yet the chapter ends with an unexpected promise: YHWH will restore Moav's fortunes in the latter days — judgment is not the final word even for Moav.

faq.question: Why does YHWH warn the remnant not to go to Mitzrayim even though it seems safer?
faq.answer: YHWH's logic in Yirmeyahu 42:15-18 is consistent: if the sword, famine, and pestilence you fear in Yehudah make you flee to Mitzrayim, those same instruments of YHWH's judgment will find you there. Mitzrayim is not outside YHWH's reach. The only safety is in the land YHWH designated for them, under the covenant. Flight to Mitzrayim — the place of their ancestors' slavery — is a return to the wrong starting point.

faq.question: How does Yirmeyahu 43:8-13's symbolic act at Tahpanhes connect to Babylon?
faq.answer: Yirmeyahu's symbolic act of hiding stones in the clay pavement at the entrance of Pharaoh's palace at Tahpanhes is a prophetic sign: Nebuchadnezzar will set his throne on those very stones when he conquers Mitzrayim. The act says: the place you fled to for safety will become Babylon's throne room. YHWH's judgment reaches Mitzrayim too.

faq.question: What happened to Yirmeyahu after the fall of Yerushalayim?
faq.answer: Nebuchadnezzar gave specific orders to treat Yirmeyahu well. After the city fell, Yirmeyahu was found among the deportees at Ramah and given the choice to go to Babylon or stay in the land. He chose to stay with Gedalyahu at Mitzpah. After Gedalyahu's murder, the surviving remnant forced Yirmeyahu (and Barukh) to accompany them to Mitzrayim. Yirmeyahu's last recorded words are in Mitzrayim, still prophesying to a community that refuses to listen.

faq.question: Why did Yirmeyahu describe the Yehudites in Mitzrayim as 'knowing whose word will stand'?
faq.answer: In Yirmeyahu 44:28-29, YHWH says the few who escape Mitzrayim will return to Yehudah, 'and all the remnant of Yehudah who came to Mitzrayim shall know whose word will stand — mine or theirs.' This is the ultimate verification test: they claimed YHWH's word through Yirmeyahu was false and their own plan was right. History itself will adjudicate the dispute. YHWH's word will stand; theirs will not.
